_purpose: Emerging theme radar. The client's instruction: space data centers was an EXAMPLE of a class - themes with low absolute chatter and rising interest, where the upside is caught early. This file tracks those themes between cycles, so the hunt is systematic rather than whatever I happened to think of that week. Reviewed every three weeks. IPS 3b.

_scoring.chatter: LOW / MEDIUM / HIGH - absolute mainstream coverage. LOW is what we want.
_scoring.trajectory: RISING / FLAT / FALLING - direction of interest. RISING + LOW is the target quadrant.
_scoring.capital_committed: Has real money moved? Funding rounds, capex line items, regulatory filings. Money moves before articles do.
_scoring.vehicle_quality: GOOD / DILUTED / NONE - is there a public company whose economics actually concentrate the theme? This is the test most themes fail.
_scoring.time_to_pnl: When does this hit an income statement?

_review_cadence: Every three weeks. Scheduled task fires on the 1st and 22nd of each month.

_execution_constraint:
DISCOVERED 2026-11-22, and it bounds what a scheduled radar run can do. This session runs in a cloud sandbox behind a policy-enforcing egress proxy. yfinance - the desk's own price source, used by engine/data.py - fails here with 'curl (7) CONNECT tunnel failed, response 403': the Yahoo market-data hosts are not on this session's allowlist. The proxy documentation is explicit that a 403 is a policy denial to be reported rather than routed around, so it was not worked around. Web fetches of stockanalysis.com do work, but that source served a 2026-10-26 snapshot for FPS (four weeks stale, against a stock whose 50-day moving average sits 36% above that snapshot price) and could not be fetched at all for ACCV.

CONSEQUENCE: a scheduled cloud run can read filings, releases, transcripts and the repo's own SEC Form 4 screener, and can therefore DISCOVER and VERIFY themes. It cannot reliably run IPS 3a, because the gate needs a current price. IPS 8 forbids a trade at a price I cannot source from live market data, and IPS 3a says missing data is a rejection and not a pass. Both rules point the same way, so the correct output of this run is candidates with gates pending, not trades. POWL is the exception only because stockanalysis.com happened to serve a current 2026-11-20 close for it.

FIX, for the client to decide on: either run the gate step inside GitHub Actions, where the daily marking job already reaches market data without trouble, or treat gate-running as interactive-session work and let the scheduled radar hand it a queue. Do not 'solve' this by letting a scheduled run gate a name on a four-week-old price.

themes.name: Co-packaged optics / silicon photonics
themes.thesis: The AI bottleneck is moving from the chip to the interconnect between chips. Copper is running out of headroom on power and latency at cluster scale, forcing optics directly into the package. Broadcom's framing is the tell: 'our switches and XPUs are going to be lower power with optics than with copper' - optics justify themselves on efficiency, not just bandwidth.

The Open Compute Interconnect standard was founded by AMD, Broadcom, NVIDIA, Meta, Microsoft and OpenAI together. Samsung and ST are bringing silicon photonics to 300mm wafer platforms. None of this was rechecked in this cycle or the last one.

themes.name: Power transformers and grain-oriented electrical steel
themes.thesis: A real, well-documented hard constraint on the AI buildout: power transformer lead times went from ~50 weeks in 2021 to ~120 weeks by 2024 (Wood Mackenzie), large units run 80-210 weeks, prices are up 60-80% since Jan 2020, and only ~20% of US demand can be met domestically. It slows the PACE of the buildout and favours the supply-constrained names. The 2026-08-14 correction stands: the constraint is real, the '30-50% of 2026 capacity cancelled' demand threat is not supported. See the note below.
themes.capital_committed:

vehicles.FPS:
NEW CANDIDATE 2026-11-22, AND IT OVERTURNS THIS THEME'S STANDING CONCLUSION. Forgent Power Solutions, NYSE, IPO'd 2026-02-05 at $27 raising about $1.5B. It designs and manufactures dry-type and liquid-filled transformers, switchgear, switchboards, panelboards, remote power panels, generator connection cabinets, tap boxes, automatic transfer switches, eHouses, power skids and PDUs, across ten campuses in the US and Mexico. Roughly 91% of FY2025 revenue was engineered-to-order. FY2025 end-market mix: data centres 42%, grid and utility 23%, industrial 19%. It carries a President of Transformers as a named officer. On venue and liquidity it clears IPS 8 comfortably - NYSE listed, market cap in the $7-8B range, 20-day average volume about 9.9M shares, which is roughly $250M a day against the $2M floor. This is the vehicle that the 2026-09-13 cycle concluded did not exist.

WHY IT IS ON THE RADAR RATHER THAN IN THE BOOK. Two independent Tier A confirmations are in hand. Tier A 4: the SEC-filed Q1 FY2027 release above, with guidance raised. Tier A 1: an insider CLUSTER, from this repo's own Form 4 screener run on 2026-11-22 - five insiders, $2.29M, all dated 2026-11-16/17, which is four days after the earnings release and about three and a half weeks after the share price collapsed. CEO and director Gary Niederpruem $334,261; newly promoted CFO Amy Ard $299,996; Chief Legal Officer Tyson Hottinger $244,956; director Neel Bhatia $199,121. IPS 3 A1 weights a cluster above a single large buy and CEO/CFO above other officers, and this is a cluster containing both. The Chief Legal Officer participating is the detail worth dwelling on, given what the share price has been reacting to.

THE BEAR CASE, HELD TO THE SAME STANDARD (IPS 4). On 2026-10-22 CFO Ryan Fiedler stepped down less than nine months after the IPO and the stock fell more than 23% in a day to a record low below its $27 IPO price, about 63% below its 2026-06-22 intraday high of $66. The stated reason, as reported, was to spend more time with his family, moving to an external consulting role, with Amy Ard - EVP of Finance since January and part of the leadership since founding - promoted internally. CRITICAL CAVEAT: that account comes from secondary reporting, not from the company's own 8-K. No accounting issue, restatement, control weakness or disagreement was mentioned in what I read; equally, none was explicitly denied, and I did not read the 8-K Item 5.02. What IS verified from a company filing is that the new CFO raised full-year guidance three weeks later and then bought $300k of stock, which is close to the opposite of what an accounting problem looks like. Analyst targets have been cut hard regardless - Jefferies $47 to $36, Morgan Stanley $51 to $45, JPMorgan $56 to $49 - against a consensus of $53.75 from 12 analysts at Strong Buy. Structurally: total debt about $704M, debt/equity 1.05, a tax receivable agreement payable of $483.0M, short interest 8.33% of float, and Neos Partners LP retains majority voting control through a dual-class structure, which makes this a controlled company under NYSE rules. The TRA and the control structure have not been analysed at all.

themes.note:
THE 2026-08-14 CORRECTION, UNCHANGED AND STILL LOAD-BEARING. I originally flagged '30-50% of announced data center capacity may slip' as a risk to this desk's AI book on the strength of one Medium post. On verification: the Currence 5GW denominator is off by multiples per SemiAnalysis, whose satellite imagery showed the top two hyperscalers alone exceeding it; the cancellations cluster in early-stage speculative announcements lacking site control, financing or interconnection; SemiAnalysis's own year-end 2026 North America self-build forecast moved about 1% over six months; and the meme traces to an April 2026 Bloomberg piece about Chinese electrical parts, sharpened downstream. 'Delayed' is also not 'cancelled'. The claim was still circulating in SEO content as of 2026-09-13 with no new primary source behind it. NOT RE-SEARCHED THIS CYCLE, so I cannot say whether it is still circulating; what I can say is that nothing found this cycle supports it, and that repetition is not corroboration.

HAMMOND'S MARGIN QUESTION IS ANSWERED, AND THE ANSWER IS REASSURING. The open question was whether Hammond's pattern - revenue +45%, EPS down from $1.12 to $0.79 - was Hammond-specific or what happens to everyone selling into this shortage. Two US-listed data points this cycle say Hammond-specific. Powell: Q4 revenue +33% with gross margin UP to 34.9% from 31.4% and EPS up to $2.23 from $1.41. Forgent: revenue +69% with net margin UP to 11.5% from 5.5%. Both expanded margin while scaling volume. So this theme is not merely a revenue story with no profit in it - at least not for everyone. CAVEAT ON THE LIMITS OF THAT: two companies is not an industry, Forgent's gross margin did slip (about 33.1% from about 34.6% by arithmetic on the release, the release itself not stating the percentages) and its adjusted EBITDA margin fell to 21.9% from 23.0% even while beating its own expectations. Volume is still arriving faster than margin at the gross line. The direction of travel is good; the question is downgraded from open to monitored, not closed.

vehicles.POWL:
VALUATION GATE RUN AND PASSED 2026-11-22. This closes the highest-value open question on this list, which had been open since 2026-09-13. Inputs, from stockanalysis.com citing S&P Global, page last updated 2026-11-21 against the 2026-11-20 close - current, not stale. Price $148.18. Market cap $5.40B. Trailing P/E 24.53. Forward P/E 19.01. EPS TTM $6.04. Revenue TTM $1.26B. Consensus target $228.75 from 4 analysts at Buy.
  Test 1, consensus upside floor 15%: +54.4%. PASS.
  Test 2, growth-adjusted multiple ceiling 2.0: 19.01 / 24.94 (3-year consensus EPS growth forecast) = 0.76. Cross-checked with the IPS 3a derived method, (24.53 / 19.01) - 1 = 29.0% implied forward growth, giving 19.01 / 29.0 = 0.66. Both well inside the ceiling. PASS.
  Test 3, earnings direction: forward P/E 19.01 sits BELOW trailing 24.53, so consensus expects earnings to RISE. No adverse comment required. PASS.
Recorded in research/valuation.json with gate PASS.

AND YET NO TRADE, FOR A REASON THAT IS NOT THE VALUATION. IPS 3 requires at least two independent confirmations with at least one from Tier A. Powell has one, clearly: Tier A 4, its own filed results. The second is missing. There is no insider cluster - Powell does not appear in this repo's Form 4 screener run - no verified 13F accumulation, and the only estimate-revision evidence available points the WRONG way: Cantor Fitzgerald cut its target to $178 from $235 on 2026-11-20 and holds a Neutral rating, and consensus itself fell from $267.50 on 2026-10-26 to $228.75. IPS 3 B5 says explicitly that upward EPS revisions matter more than headline targets and that a revision is an analyst admitting they were wrong - the revisions here are downward. Overriding the signal-count minimum is permitted under IPS 5 but would spend an override slot to buy a name whose analyst revisions are falling, which is not conviction, it is impatience. The honest state is: gate passed, confirmation count short, no trade.

WHAT CANTOR'S CUT ACTUALLY WAS, because it would be easy to misread as a demand warning. Per the reporting, analyst Manish Somaiya cited near-term startup inefficiencies at new capacity, and Cantor framed it as a timing issue rather than a change in the margin-improvement framework, adding that a follow-up with the CFO strengthened its confidence in the FY2027 setup. The CFO's own language on the call was that the company is 'exiting the backlog at about a 30% clip', that the FY2026 margin profile is 'sustainable in Fiscal 2027, as the pricing environment remains stable', and that new facilities could create a brief productivity air pocket, with a 'seasonally soft' fiscal first quarter. So: a margin-timing cut, not a demand cut.

SOURCE CAVEAT I WILL NOT PAPER OVER: the transcript I relied on was verbatim only for the prepared remarks. The Q&A quotes above come from a model-extracted summary of an AI-assisted transcript that itself reported speaker-attribution errors. They are directionally consistent with the company's own release, which I did read in full, but they are not primary and should be checked against the real transcript before they are used to support a position.
vehicles.POWL_data_centre_question:
ANSWERED 2026-11-22, AND THE ANSWER CUTS AGAINST THE CONVENIENT READING. The open question was whether Powell's data-centre order mix is durable or a single lumpy award. Management's own framing, from the Q4 call: CEO Brett Cope said of data centres 'I still use the word opportunistic' and 'The visibility is good, not as good as the other two' - the other two being LNG and electric utility. He also said Powell has seen no de-bookings, only scope changes, and that scope risk 'probably does go up' on configure-to-order work. The order evidence agrees: the big Q4 award was LNG at about $250M, with data centre at about $85M, and the LNG order spans roughly three years. Q4 revenue by market: Commercial and Other Industrial +179% - which is where data centre sits, 'driven predominantly by' it per the call summary, though the release never states a data-centre revenue figure - Oil and Gas +24%, Electric Utility +22%, while Petrochemical fell 49% and Light Rail 24%.

SO: Powell is a grid, LNG and industrial electrification vehicle with genuine data-centre upside. It is NOT a data-centre pure-play, and management ranks data-centre visibility BELOW its other two growth markets. The 2026-09-13 caveat - do not let the convenience of a listed vehicle blur what it actually sells - was right, and is now confirmed in management's own words rather than merely suspected. This does not weaken the POWL case; it relabels it. A name that passes the gate on LNG and utility demand and gets data centre for free is a perfectly good position. Calling it an AI-infrastructure play would be the CLF error in a new costume.
vehicles.POWL_backlog_conversion: NEW DETAIL, AND THE ONE REAL NEGATIVE IN THE PRINT. Of the $2.7B backlog, the CFO put $1.3B as scheduled to convert in FY2027 - about 48%. A year earlier, about 60% of a $1.4B backlog, a little over $800M, was expected within twelve months. So the conversion SHARE fell while the absolute FY2027 number rose about 62%. The CFO called the lower ratio 'just a function of math and the level of bookings that we've accepted', and most of the remainder is the multi-year LNG award. Read carefully, that is backlog lengthening rather than stalling - CEO: 'Our visibility now extends well into fiscal 2028, and in some cases beyond.' But it does mean the orders-to-revenue gap closes more slowly than a naive read of +162% orders would suggest, and the old tripwire wanted that gap closing from the revenue side. Q4 revenue +33% says it is. Both figures come from the model-extracted part of the transcript and want primary confirmation.
vehicles.ACCV:
NEW CANDIDATE 2026-11-22. Accelevation Holdings, NASDAQ, based in Miamisburg, Ohio, IPO'd in early October 2026 - it raised about $540M priced BELOW its marketed range, with net primary proceeds reported around $171M. It designs, manufactures and installs modular, factory-built power and white-space infrastructure for data centres and self-performs the installation: the SkyBridge modular platform, techFrame steel structures, thermal management, remote power panels, branch circuit whips and power distribution units. Customers are hyperscalers, neoclouds and colocation providers; management says it sells to all five hyperscalers but names none.

WHY IT MATTERS: this is the purest listed vehicle this radar has found for the inside of the data centre. Where CLF buried a monopoly inside commodity steel and POWL sells mostly to LNG and utilities, essentially all of Accelevation's revenue is data-centre infrastructure. Vehicle quality is the axis that kills most themes on this list, and this one passes it cleanly. Customer concentration is also better than expected for a company this young: management said only two customers were a double-digit percentage of Q3 bookings and the largest was under 20% of Q3 revenue. On IPS 8 it clears - NASDAQ, market cap around $3.1B, average volume about 1.3M shares against a low-teens share price, so roughly $18M a day against the $2M floor.

WHY IT IS NOT A BUY, AND THE INSIDER SIGNAL IS WEAKER THAN IT LOOKS. The Form 4 screener flags five insiders and $8.20M, which at first glance looks like the stronger of this cycle's two clusters - CEO and director Michael Rubiera $3.66M, directors Ginger Jones $180k, Paul Donahue $126k and Howard Heckes $90k, COO Brent Jewell $45k. But every single purchase is dated 2026-10-01, the IPO window, and there is no recorded insider buying since. That is cornerstone participation in the offering, not open-market accumulation in response to a price decline, and those are different signals: directors buying into their own IPO is a condition of the deal as much as a view on the price. Contrast FPS, where the cluster is dated after both the collapse and the earnings release. Meanwhile the stock hit a new one-year low on 2026-11-20. Insiders have not been seen adding into that weakness. Six weeks of public history, an IPO priced below range, and a gate that cannot be run because stockanalysis.com would not serve the page to this session, is not a buy. Also note the company is only marginally profitable - about $3M of net income on $202M of quarterly revenue - so a P/E gate will be distorted and the IPS 3a treatment needs deciding before it is applied rather than after.

themes.name: How the AI buildout is actually being financed
themes.thesis: Capex is growing faster than the revenue it supports. That gap has to be financed somewhere - vendor financing, private credit, SPVs, debt. Follow the money and you find both a risk indicator for the whole desk and possibly a beneficiary. This is the theme most likely to matter to this desk as a WARNING rather than an opportunity.
themes.capital_committed:
CAPEX GUIDANCE RE-CHECKED 2026-11-22, VIA AN AGGREGATOR QUOTING EARNINGS CALLS - secondary, not primary. Calendar-2026 guidance midpoints for the four largest US hyperscalers: Alphabet about $200B, Amazon about $220B, Microsoft about $170B, Meta about $140B (narrowed to $135-145B), totalling about $730B. Supply, not demand, is the stated constraint - Alphabet cited a 'supply-constrained environment' and began renting third-party capacity late in Q3; Microsoft said 'customer demand continues to exceed available supply'.

Project Stargate up to $500B over four years with $9.6B already drawn across two construction loans for the Abilene, Texas campus alone. themes.note:
WHY THIS MATTERS TO THIS DESK SPECIFICALLY, and the reason has changed shape. In September the argument was that the AI book, nine names deep in the buildout, was quietly inheriting interest-rate sensitivity that no individual thesis mentioned - a correlated risk hiding inside an apparently diversified book. That risk has now partly expressed itself: six of those names hit automatic stops between 2026-09-14 and 2026-11-10 and the AI book is -15.1% from its high-water mark. The correlation was real. What has NOT been established is that financing was the mechanism.

THE DISCIPLINED READING, AND I WANT TO BE CAREFUL HERE BECAUSE THE TEMPTING STORY IS RIGHT THERE. A 25-30% drawdown in the semis complex alongside a theme file warning about leverage practically invites the conclusion that the financing risk came home. But I did not check credit spreads on AI-infrastructure paper this cycle, I did not check loan-to-cost ratios on new financings, and I have no evidence of an anchor tenant failing to take contracted capacity. Three of the four tripwires below were not examined at all. Claiming the monitor was vindicated on the strength of a price decline that coincided with it would be exactly the error of the 2026-08-14 capacity-cancellation episode - a comfortable-sounding narrative accepted because it sounded prudent. The price fell. Why it fell is not established by this file.

WHAT THE CAPEX CHECK ACTUALLY FOUND, AND IT POINTS THE OTHER WAY. No verified cut at any of the four. All four guide 2027 up, and both Alphabet and Microsoft describe themselves as supply-constrained rather than demand-constrained. One item deserves care rather than dismissal: Microsoft's calendar-2026 plan was reported reduced to about $170B because third-party capacity arrived LATE, with the prior figure not stated. A reduction caused by capacity arriving late is a timing slip that pushes spend into 2027, which is what Microsoft's own 'accelerate in the second half of the fiscal year' language describes. It is NOT a demand cut. It is also not primary-sourced, and the aggregator that reported it noted Microsoft's shift to operating leases moves some building out of reported capex - which means the headline number and the real spend are drifting apart in a way that makes any single capex figure less informative than it looks.

STILL NOT ESTABLISHED, AND NOW TWO CYCLES OLD: what share of hyperscaler capex is debt-financed. J.P. Morgan's published work gave no explicit debt-versus-cash-flow percentage and nothing found since does either. Three large debt deals do not establish a system-wide ratio and I am not going to infer one. The aggregator asserts that free cash flow turned negative at several of these companies and that all four issued bonds this year; that is the aggregator's analysis, not company language, and it is the right thread to pull next cycle from the cash flow statements themselves, which is a primary source and is actually reachable from a scheduled run.

NOTE ON CAPEX FIGURES, CARRIED FORWARD: this file has at various points carried $840B, $725B, $697B and now about $730B for hyperscaler capex. They cover different baskets and different definitions. Do not stack them, average them, or quote a single 'the' capex number as though the definition were settled.

_lesson_log.lesson: Applied the verification standard asymmetrically: demanded primary sources before BUYING, accepted a Medium post before flagging a RISK. Bear claims need the same evidence bar as bull claims. A comfortable-sounding caution is still a claim.
_lesson_log.cost: None - caught before it changed any position.
_lesson_log.fix: IPS 4 now applies explicitly to risk claims as well as thesis claims.

_lesson_log.lesson: Four scheduled research runs between 2026-08-31 and 2026-09-07 reported SUCCESS and committed nothing. Roughly four hours of model time produced no durable output, and nobody noticed for two weeks because the only signal of a working system was a push notification that only fires on trades. A job that cannot write is indistinguishable from a job that found nothing, and 'no news' was read as 'nothing happening' when it actually meant 'nothing is reaching you'.
_lesson_log.cost: Two weeks of a stale radar and four wasted runs. No position was harmed - the daily marking and risk rules run in GitHub Actions and never stopped.
_lesson_log.fix: Scheduled runs must verify their own commit landed rather than trusting a clean exit, and must report the failure loudly if it did not. A silent success is the most dangerous possible outcome, because it looks exactly like a quiet market.

_lesson_log.lesson: The '50% of 2026 AI capacity at risk' claim, debunked here on 2026-08-14, resurfaced repeatedly in that cycle's search results - now carried by low-quality SEO content rather than any new evidence. The temptation to treat its reappearance as corroboration is real.
_lesson_log.cost: None - recognised on sight because the August correction was written down in this file.
_lesson_log.fix: Repetition is not corroboration. Before treating a re-encountered claim as confirmed, check whether it traces to a NEW primary source or to the same original. This is the practical argument for keeping the lesson log: it is what made the claim recognisable the second time.

_lesson_log.lesson: The write failure recurred, and the fix written down on 2026-09-13 did not prevent it. Three scheduled runs - 2026-10-01, 2026-10-22, 2026-11-01 - left no commit touching this file. `git log -- research/watchlist.json` returns exactly one commit in the repo's history. The file's own _next_review said 2026-10-04 and it went ten weeks past that untouched. Writing the correct remedy into a lesson log is not the same as the remedy being in force: the September entry prescribed that runs verify their own commit landed, and nothing in the system made that happen.
_lesson_log.cost: Ten weeks of a radar that was not merely stale but actively wrong - it asserted BOUGHT and HELD status for COHR, ALAB and NVDA for between five and ten weeks after each was sold. A reader checking the Radar tab would have believed the desk held three positions it did not hold.
_lesson_log.fix: Verification has to be mechanical, not intentional. This run fetches origin and greps `git log origin/main` for its own commit hash before reporting success, and sends the digest unconditionally - including on a nothing-found cycle - because silence was what let the previous failure run for two weeks. If the push fails, the complete file content goes into the run summary so the work survives outside the repo. Worth considering beyond this run: a dashboard that displayed _last_review as an age in days rather than a date would have made ten weeks visible at a glance.

_lesson_log.lesson: The radar was never reconciled against the portfolio state files, so it kept describing positions the engine had already sold. Worse, the two themes it was most confident about were the ones it was wrong about: co-packaged optics was recorded BOUGHT on the strength of COHR and ALAB, and orbital compute rested on 'NVDA HELD - the cleanest exposure, and free inside a position owned for other reasons'. All three had been stopped out. The phrase 'free exposure inside a position held for other reasons' was the specific trap: it is only free while the position is held, and a stop-loss on the other reasons takes the free thing with it silently.
_lesson_log.cost: No direct financial cost - the stops executed correctly and on time. The cost was epistemic: the research file and the portfolio disagreed for ten weeks and nothing in the system noticed.
_lesson_log.fix: Every cycle now reconciles every vehicle marked BOUGHT or HELD against state/*.json before any new research is done, and records the sale date and realized loss rather than quietly deleting the claim. A theme whose exposure was removed by an automatic stop should be flagged as a decision for the client, not silently re-scored - the desk currently holds a thesis it has no way of expressing, and that is a fact somebody should choose about rather than inherit.

_lesson_log.lesson: On 2026-09-13 I concluded that no liquid US-listed pure-play on power transformers exists, and recorded the pass as a result - correctly in principle, since recording a pass is a result. The conclusion was wrong. Forgent Power Solutions had been listed on the NYSE since 2026-02-05, makes dry-type and liquid-filled transformers, took 42% of FY2025 revenue from data centres and trades around $250M a day. The method is what failed: I checked the names I already knew - Hammond, Cleveland-Cliffs, Powell - and when none of them fitted, I concluded the category was empty. A company that IPO'd nine months earlier is invisible to a search framed around established names, and a recent IPO into exactly the theme under examination is the single most likely place for an undiscovered vehicle to be hiding. This radar exists to find low-chatter vehicles and it walked past one by looking only where it had looked before.
_lesson_log.cost: Nine months of not watching a name that is now about 60% off its high with a five-insider cluster buying into the weakness. No capital was committed either way, so the cost is opportunity and unquantifiable - but 'no vehicle exists' is a conclusion that closes a theme, and closing a theme wrongly is expensive in a way that is hard to see later.
_lesson_log.fix: Before concluding that a theme has no investable vehicle, screen recent IPOs and new listings in that sector explicitly. 'I could not find one' and 'one does not exist' are different statements and the second needs the first to have searched somewhere the answer could have been. Generalised: the vehicle-quality axis is the one IPS 3b warns I will be most tempted to fudge, and it turns out there are two ways to fudge it - stretching a bad vehicle to fit, which the CLF entry guards against, and declaring the category empty without looking properly, which nothing guarded against.

_lesson_log.lesson: A scheduled cloud run cannot source a market price, and that structurally limits what this task can produce. yfinance - the desk's own price source in engine/data.py - fails from this session with a 403 policy denial at the egress proxy. The documented instruction for a 403 is to report the blocked host rather than route around it, so it was not routed around. The one web source that did respond, stockanalysis.com, served a four-week-old snapshot for FPS and refused the ACCV page entirely. The temptation was to gate FPS on a 2026-10-26 price of $25.12 while the same page showed a 50-day moving average of $34.08 - which is to say, on a price known to be wrong.
_lesson_log.cost: One cycle's delay on the most actionable candidate this radar has produced. FPS has two independent Tier A confirmations and probably clears the gate; it is not being bought because a scheduled run cannot honestly run the gate, not because of anything about the company.
_lesson_log.fix: Treat gate-running and theme-discovery as separate jobs on separate infrastructure. A scheduled cloud run can read filings, releases and the repo's own Form 4 screener, so it should discover, verify and queue. The gate arithmetic belongs where market data is reachable - GitHub Actions, where the daily marking job already gets prices without trouble, or an interactive session. What must not happen is a scheduled run gating a name on a stale price because the alternative was returning empty-handed. IPS 3a already says missing data is a rejection and not a pass; this is that rule meeting an infrastructure limit rather than an information gap, and the answer is the same.
